title: Moon, sun, and the guru
hookLine: a moon, a sun, a road between, and a real argument about who teaches it
carry: some practices are handed on, guru to student
tomorrow: what color is the lotus at the navel? not the one on the poster.

lines: A ROAD BETWEEN, AND AN ARGUMENT.
cards: A subway map is lines as much as stations. The Sat-Cakra-Nirupana draws its lines too: a moon on the left, a sun on the right, and a road straight up the middle, with the lotuses strung along it.
And around those lines sits a real disagreement, one you could still hear today between two yoga teachers sharing a coffee.

teach.h: NADIS: MOON LEFT, SUN RIGHT, ROAD BETWEEN.
teach.b: The lines are nadis, usually translated channels. Ida runs on the left, linked with the moon; Pingala on the right, with the sun; Sushumna up the center, carrying the lotuses.

The Hatha Yoga Pradipika ties a breathing practice to them: in through one nostril, out through the other, then back again, a way of cleansing the nadis. And it stresses learning such practice from a guru.
That's a deep Hindu teaching with a name: guru-shishya parampara, knowledge handed on, teacher to student, in an unbroken line. The Mahabharata tells a hard story about it.
A young hunter, Ekalavya, asks the great teacher Drona to train him in archery, and is turned away.

So he shapes an image of Drona from clay, practices before it, and grows so skilled he outshines Drona's star pupil, Arjuna. Drona asks for his teacher's fee: the boy's right thumb. Ekalavya gives it.
Readers have argued over it ever since, and the argument is still alive.

teach.h: KEEP IT WITH A TEACHER, OR SHARE IT?
teach.b: One view hears devotion: a teacher matters so much that even his image can teach, so keep practices with someone who can see what you're doing.
The other hears a door shut on someone who deserved to learn: the basics belong to everyone.

teach.h: ONE MAP, TWO WAYS TO HAND IT ON.
teach.b: Both honor the same map, and the same reverence for the teacher. They differ on who should hold it, and how it's handed on.
The science seat adds one quiet note: the breath is real, whatever a person decides the channels are.

how: Alternate-nostril breathing, nadi shodhana, is taught in hatha yoga classes; in traditional lineages, breath practices tied to the nadis are learned under a teacher's guidance.

games.q: what does “the chakras as a map” mean?
o: a chart of the body's nerves, renamed in Sanskrit
a calendar that tracks the moon and the sun
a map whose lines run moon, sun, and the road between

games.q: the map's lines — tap the pairs.
p: the left channel, linked with the moon
the right channel, linked with the sun
learned before a clay image of Drona

s: everyone in the tradition agrees on how widely to teach breath practices
some keep them with a teacher; others share the basics widely. both honor the same map.
Ida is linked with the moon and Pingala with the sun
and Sushumna, the road between them, carries the lotuses.
in the Mahabharata, Drona gladly took Ekalavya as a student
Drona turned him away; Ekalavya practiced before a clay image of him, then gave his thumb as the teacher's fee.

games.q: you think simple breathing should be shared with everyone. a friend disagrees. what's the best case for her side, keeping it with a teacher?
o: the manual stresses a teacher's guidance; care with a practice is a form of respect.
teachers just want to charge money for something that's free.
breathing exercises are dangerous for every person, every time.
games.why: that's the view as its holders put it. the other two make it a cartoon. you can keep your view and still state hers well.

practice: Think of one teacher who handed you something you still use. Join your palms, or bow your head a little, and say their name and a thank-you inwardly, the way many Hindus honor the guru before study.
If you don't pray, simply hold their face in mind with gratitude for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The chakras as a map: its lines are nadis, Ida with the moon, Pingala with the sun, and Sushumna, the road between.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a channel; the lines on the yoga map.

carryVoice: Your line: some practices are handed on, guru to student. One map, two ways to hand it on. Sleep well.

sources.ref: Sat-Cakra-Nirupana (Ida and Pingala on the left and right, linked with moon and sun; Sushumna in the middle; the lotuses placed along it)
Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.7–10 (breathing in through one nostril and out through the other to cleanse the nadis); the text's stress on the guru's instruction
Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ekalavya is refused by Drona, practices before a clay image of him, and gives his right thumb as the teacher's fee)
